BREAKING: 221 US trucking companies have filed for bankruptcy so far in 2026, on track for the highest annual total in 23 years.

This marks the 3rd consecutive year with at least 220 bankruptcies.

By comparison, annual bankruptcies were below 100 in both 2021 and 2022.

Furthermore, ~66% of small US trucking firms, typically operating 20 or fewer trucks, reported flat or declining revenue YoY, according to a Truckstop and Bloomberg survey of hundreds of carriers.

At the same time, ~40% expect to leave the industry or are unsure of their future over the next 6 months.

This comes as surging diesel prices, rising insurance premiums, and higher interest rates are increasingly squeezing smaller trucking companies.

The US trucking industry needs help.

BREAKING: US data center construction spending jumped +90% YoY in September, to a record annualized rate of $96.5 billion.

This also marks the largest YoY increase in 10 years.

This figure is now risen more than +60% YoY for 4 consecutive months.

Since the start of 2024, data center construction spending has nearly quadrupled.

Meanwhile, general office construction spending fell -8% YoY in September, to $46.0 billion, near its lowest level since January 2016.

This brought the gap between data center and general office construction spending to a record $50.5 billion.

Overall, US construction spending fell -1.9% MoM in September, its biggest monthly decline since April 2020.

The AI infrastructure buildout is transforming the US economy.

BREAKING: US M2 money supply jumped +$113 billion in August, to a record $23.41 trillion.

YoY, M2 grew +5.7%, its largest YoY increase since May 2022.

This also marks the 3rd consecutive month of accelerating growth.

This is 89% above the average monthly growth of +$72 billion recorded throughout 2025.

US money creation is gaining momentum.

BREAKING: The US manufacturing sector added +19,000 jobs in October, its 3rd-largest monthly increase since November 2023.

This also marks the 5th consecutive monthly gain, the longest streak since 2022.

Over this period, the manufacturing sector has added +86,000 jobs, bringing total employment to 12.68 million, its highest since December 2024.

This follows a decline of -323,000 jobs between January 2023 and December 2025.

Despite the recent recovery, US manufacturing employment remains 222,000 jobs below its January 2023 level.

US manufacturing employment is seeing some much needed relief.

The global rate hike cycle is accelerating:

~45% of global central banks have raised interest rates over the last 3 months, the largest total in 3 years.

This proportion has surged +40 percentage points since March.

By comparison, between 2024 and March 2026, more central banks were cutting rates than raising them.

Furthermore, global central banks have delivered 42 rate hikes over the last 6 months, the largest number since late 2023.

This figure has quadrupled over the last 7 months and is comparable to the rate hike cycle seen in 2019.

The global monetary tightening cycle is gaining momentum.

BREAKING: The US unemployment rate has remained below 5.0% for 62 consecutive months, its 2nd-longest streak on record.

This trails only the 64-month stretch recorded during the 1960s and 1970s.

This is also 20 months longer than the 42-month streak that ended during the 2020 pandemic.

The current run began in September 2021, when the unemployment rate fell to 4.7%, from 5.1% in August 2021.

To put this into perspective, the unemployment rate has averaged 5.6% since the start of the century.

The US job market is still remarkably resilient.

History says last week's drop was a buying opportunity.

On Thursday, the S&P 500 declined -4.4%, its largest daily drop since April 2025.

Before that day, the index recorded 56 one-day declines of at least -4.0% since 1952.

Following such drops, the S&P 500 has gained +1.0% on average over the next week.

By comparison, its average weekly return across all periods has been +0.2%.

Over the next month, the index has averaged a gain of +2.0%, compared with +0.8% across all periods.

Over the following 3 months, the S&P 500 has averaged +6.7%, more than triple the historical average of +2.2%.

History suggests the market is set for a meaningful rebound.

To put this into perspective, this percentage peaked at ~10.8% in 2012, following the 2008 Financial Crisis.

The commercial real estate crisis is still worsening.

This was the week it felt like investors finally threw in the white towel on the AI trade.

The S&P 500 was down just 2.7% for the week, but it felt far worse. The real damage wasn't in the index. It was in the hedge fund world, where what looked like a capitulation moment triggered a cascade of forced selling across hedge funds, leveraged ETFs, and CTAs. The Nasdaq 100 (NDX/QQQ) finished down 5% for the week, with more than 100% of that decline occurring in just two hours on Thursday, between 8:30 and 10:30 a.m. New York time.

The magnitude of the deleveraging was extraordinary. Volatility spiked, put-call ratios reached extremes, trading volumes exploded, and hedge funds cut exposure at a historic pace. Hedge fund closure rumors went viral.

And I was buying into the panic.  

In this week's video, I explain why I would try and catch a falling knife and why I believe we're witnessing a market structure deleveraging event rather than a breakdown in AI fundamentals or the economy. I go through the data behind the forced selling, the factor signals I'm watching for exhaustion, and why the midterm results may have actually reduced the risk of an AI bubble.

I also explore the changing market structure, the emerging importance of factor rotations, and why declining liquidity headwinds could be a significant positive for AI, Bitcoin, and gold.

The AI revolution is a long-duration investment opportunity being traded in an increasingly short-duration market.

Investing is becoming a counterpuncher's game. The market structure has changed forever and hedge fund leverage has forever peaked.
